\textbf{Accuracy on instructed-lie benchmarks does not identify deception: the intervention that creates the lie also changes instruction-following behavior.} \textbf{Our contribution is an operational identification audit for behavioral LLM benchmarks}---whose general form we name the \textbf{Elicitation--Construct Confounding Principle}, with behavioral deception detection as one instantiation---\textbf{together with empirical evidence that the common instructed-lie paradigm produces large, reproducible attribution failures across three detector paradigms, and that benchmark design can determine which behavioral signal appears to constitute ``deception detection''.} \textbf{We do not ask whether LLMs can detect deception; we ask whether current benchmarks provide evidence that they do.} The reason is structural: \textbf{no experiment that intervenes only on the instruction can separate a detector response mediated by deception from one mediated by instruction-following}, both being descendants of that instruction. A deception-attribution reading needs $\tau_D$, which the identified $\tau_E$---the \emph{instruction}'s effect---neither bounds nor signs, so no gain in accuracy or scale resolves it. \textbf{This is an identification problem, not a generalization one: generalization can be perfect while identification fails.} The audit has five parts: \textbf{one necessary construct-validity test no instructed design can supply}, three alternative-explanation diagnostics and one robustness test. Fixed elicitation itself is not new---trained belief-verified organisms have it---but not as the \emph{construct-validity criterion} for reading instructed-benchmark accuracy.

Reimplemented from scratch, the standard black-box detector reaches 81.7\% instructed and 53.7\% under identical prompts; a pre-registered replication on a disjoint claim set and probe bank \textbf{leaves no detectable above-chance discrimination on any of the six targets} (97.0\%$\to$\textbf{43.3\%}), as does a white-box linear probe on residual activations in two model families, at 100.0\% instructed, at chance equalized, and matched by surface features (92.5--99.0\%). \textbf{The accuracy the benchmark is scored on is reachable with no learned features at all}: a parameter-free lexical rule reaches 69--80\%---\emph{surface-accessible accuracy}, not a decomposition of the detector's signal. Auditing both public rollout releases for the one criterion that removes the confound: \textbf{nine of ten rollout sets cannot supply it} for a deployed-observable rule; on the tenth our rule is \textbf{null} while \textbf{the corpus authors' own judge, on the same visible text, does separate deception there} (AUROC 0.71/0.94), so the null is the instrument's, not the criterion's; scoring the \emph{hidden} scaffold instead reports $+84.3$\,pp---\textbf{annotation-channel leakage}. A second release---35 cells, five generator families, pre-registered---fails differently: its label grades the very text both instruments read, so passing is \textbf{construct recovery}. We claim identification, not attribution, and \textbf{equalization may remove the deception with the confound}. Because \textbf{no public release we audited supplies all five}, we built materials that do: with deception operationalized independently of the detector's input, prior work's battery separates operationally verified deception on three of five targets---all three with power ($p\!\leq\!0.006$; two underpowered nulls)---of which \textbf{a blinded re-run replicates two and a pre-registered covariate audit withdraws one, so the standing count is one of five}, with \textbf{one of five \emph{new} targets positive}. \textbf{The instructed benchmark's most discriminative probe is inert at fixed elicitation}, and another replaces it. \textbf{The canonical benchmark fails to identify deception, while a fixed-elicitation design reveals \emph{target-dependent} deception-associated signals}---still not $\tau_D$---\textbf{rung~4 of five}. \textbf{Scope: English, instructed-roleplay evaluations, open-weight models 3B--70B.}

Write $E$ for the deception instruction, $C$ for compliance behavior, and $S$ for the detector's output. Deception is the \emph{act}: \textbf{$D\!=\!1$ iff the target asserts $p$ while holding $\neg p$}---binary, latent, and observed by no benchmark audited here. $D$, $C$, the claim's truth-value $V$ and the target's belief $B$ are all parents of $S$ (Figure~\ref{fig:dag}; §\ref{sec:belief_strata}). \paragraph{The Elicitation--Construct Confounding Principle (ECCP).} \emph{When a benchmark creates its target construct $Y$ by an intervention $E$ that also changes the elicited behavior $C$ a detector reads, no score evaluated only under $\mathrm{do}(E)$ is attributable to $Y$.} The Proposition below is that statement for $k$ unobserved mechanisms; \textbf{behavioral deception detection is the instantiation $(M_1,M_2)=(D,C)$}. \textbf{It also names an escape route a designer controls, and public corpora already take it piecewise}: of \textbf{28} pinned public corpora, \textbf{2, 21 and 3} supply each of the three properties that make a benchmark auditable on $Y$---crossing elicitation with items, recording the channel a detector reads, grading $Y$ off that channel---and \textbf{none supplies all three}, so an auditable benchmark needs no new idea, only the combination. \textbf{Outside deception the precondition is thus decidable and decided; the magnitude is measured only for deception} (EXP-AF, Appendix~\ref{app:eccp_decidability}).

Pre-registered, replicated on a disjoint claim set (Appendix~\ref{app:probe_audit}).

\subsection{Q3: Criterion 4 on Public Corpora, and on Materials Built for It (EXP-XA/XJ/XL, EXP-C4)}

\paragraph{Public corpora: an instrument-specific null, annotation-channel leakage, and construct recovery (EXP-XA/XJ, EXP-IT).} $D$ is each set's per-rollout grade, never the condition label (pre-registered). One set clears both gates---sandbagging, $n\!=\!1000$, one fixed system prompt---and there our rule is \textbf{null} ($+4.1$/$+7.7$\,pp, $p\!=\!0.32$/$0.17$) while the release's \emph{own} judge \textbf{separates operationally verified deception at fixed elicitation} (AUROC 0.71/0.94, $p\!=\!0.0001$). \textbf{The null is the instrument's, not the criterion's.} On the \emph{full} transcript the same rule looks decisive ($+84.3$\,pp, $p\!=\!0.0001$) because the mandated scaffold asks for an ``\emph{incorrect} answer''---the pattern the rule keys on---whence~(iv). On-policy insider trading fails differently: (i)--(iv) hold and a disclosure rule separates the grade by $-77.1$\,pp, but deceiving \emph{is} omitting the source, so rule and grader share evidence---\textbf{construct recovery}, whence~(v)---while against the \emph{action} label both are \textbf{null} ($+21.6$\,pp, $p\!=\!0.97$; EXP-IT2).

\paragraph{So we built one, and prior work's own battery separates deception in it (EXP-C4, \emph{pre-registered}).} One system prompt per claim presents a knowledge-screened false fact as an authoritative reference and \textbf{never instructs deception}; the target asserts it---deception, the belief screen showing it holds $\neg p$---or corrects it, $D$ graded cross-family from the \textbf{on-claim answer alone} ($\alpha\!=\!0.728$) while the detector reads only the 16-probe vector, so all of~(i)--(v) hold. \textbf{On three of five targets---all three with power---the battery separates operationally verified deception at byte-identical elicitation}: 0.650/0.807/0.903 against majority 0.575/0.594/0.682, $p\!\leq\!0.006$ under claim-grouped folds; the other two are \textbf{null and uninformative} (MDE $\ge\!0.80$)---and because the contrast reuses \emph{prior work's own} battery, a null here is partly about \textbf{that instrument's portability}, not only deception detectability. Not belief revision (H3, pre-registered). \emph{Stratified observational} at fixed $E$: deception-\emph{associated}, not $\tau_D$ (Appendix~\ref{app:crit4_ours}). A blinded, Holm-corrected re-run (EXP-C4B) replicates two of the three positives---not the weakest---and one of five \emph{new} targets (Appendix~\ref{app:crit4b}). Given the battery's own folds and null, sixteen surface covariates \textbf{beat it on Llama~3.1~8B} ($p_{\mathrm{Holm}}\!=\!0.0005$), \textbf{so that positive is withdrawn: the standing count is one of five}; elsewhere the battery leads, not separably (EXP-AE, Appendix~\ref{app:covariate_audit}). \textbf{Criterion~5 (transfer) is exploratory}: 2 of 5, not part of the argument (Appendix~\ref{app:crit4_transfer}). \textbf{Criterion~4's purpose is not to show deception is generally detectable but that the canonical benchmark's failure is not an impossibility result---and the standing 1-of-5 is itself a positive finding rather than a disappointment: once the elicitation confound is removed, detection is markedly less stable across targets than the instructed benchmark's near-ceiling accuracy suggests.}

Only correction-marker density clears reliability (Krippendorff's $\alpha\!=\!0.606$, vs.\ 0.070--0.264 for the other four); \textbf{human rating is not a premise of the identification result}---EXP-R1/R1b/R1c and the lexical audit use neither LLM-extracted features nor human ratings; transfer beyond instructed roleplay is exploratory. \textbf{We do not establish} the four negatives boxed in §\ref{sec:eval_controls}. The alternative reading---that deception is undetectable---is what (4) tests, and the evidence runs against it. The general lesson, which we name the \textbf{Elicitation--Construct Confounding Principle}, is that a benchmark label generated by an intervention can quietly become a label for the intervention itself. \textbf{Its precondition is decidable outside deception and we decide it}---on four published designs and 28 pinned corpora---\textbf{while its magnitude we measure only for behavioral deception detection} (EXP-AF, Appendix~\ref{app:eccp_decidability}).
